subject: chemistry
title: Matter and particle model
overview: Matter has mass and occupies space. Solids, liquids and gases differ in particle arrangement and motion.
example: A closed container can hold water vapour even when it looks empty.
misconception: Particles are not motionless in a solid.

subject: chemistry
title: Atoms, protons and isotopes
overview: Atomic number counts protons. Isotopes share a proton number but differ in neutron number.
example: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon isotopes.
misconception: An atom's mass number is not always its relative atomic mass.

subject: chemistry
title: Periodic table and families
overview: Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number. Group members often share characteristic valence patterns.
example: Sodium and potassium are Group 1 metals.
misconception: Hydrogen's position does not make it an alkali metal.

subject: chemistry
title: Ionic and covalent bonding
overview: Ionic models involve electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Covalent models involve shared electron pairs.
example: Sodium chloride forms an extended ionic lattice; water contains polar covalent bonds.
misconception: A chemical bond is not simply two atoms touching.

subject: chemistry
title: Mixtures and separation
overview: A mixture contains substances without a fixed chemical ratio. Separation uses differences in properties such as solubility or boiling behaviour.
example: Filter sand from salt water; then evaporate water to recover salt.
misconception: Dissolved salt will not be caught by ordinary filter paper.

subject: chemistry
title: Acids, bases and pH
overview: pH indicates hydrogen-ion activity on a logarithmic scale. Indicators change colour over particular ranges.
example: Dilute strong acid and strong base may neutralise at an equivalence point near pH 7 under ideal conditions.
misconception: An indicator endpoint is not always exactly the equivalence point.

subject: chemistry
title: Concentration and moles
overview: Amount of substance is measured in moles. For a solution, concentration in mol/L equals moles of solute divided by volume in litres.
example: 0.100 mol/L contains 0.00250 mol in 25.0 mL.
misconception: Volume in mL must be converted to litres before calculating moles.

subject: chemistry
title: Chemical equations
overview: Balanced equations conserve each type of atom and represent proportions of reacting substances.
example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
misconception: A balanced equation does not tell you reaction speed.

subject: chemistry
title: Rates and energy changes
overview: Rate describes how fast reactant concentrations change. Reactions may absorb or release energy.
example: Increasing temperature often speeds an ordinary reaction, but not every mechanism responds identically.
misconception: Catalysts do not change the overall equilibrium constant.

subject: chemistry
title: Laboratory measurement and errors
overview: Measure with appropriate apparatus, include units and estimate uncertainty. Repeat readings and distinguish systematic from random error.
example: Record burette start and end readings before calculating delivered volume.
misconception: A digital-looking number is not automatically exact.

subject: physics
title: Physical quantities and SI units
overview: Measurement combines a number and unit. SI base quantities include length, mass and time.
example: A speed of 5 m/s is not the same as 5 km/h.
misconception: Units are part of the physical answer.

subject: physics
title: Distance, displacement and velocity
overview: Distance is path length; displacement has magnitude and direction. Velocity is rate of displacement.
example: Walking around a track can give zero displacement but a nonzero distance.
misconception: Speed and velocity are not interchangeable.

subject: physics
title: Newton's laws of motion
overview: A net force changes momentum. For constant mass, F = ma is useful in an inertial reference frame.
example: Doubling the net force doubles acceleration at fixed mass.
misconception: Motion does not always require a net force.

subject: physics
title: Work, energy and power
overview: Work transfers energy when force acts through displacement. Power is energy transfer per time.
example: An electrical resistor dissipates energy at P = VI.
misconception: Energy and power have different units.

subject: physics
title: Voltage, current and resistance
overview: Voltage is electric potential difference; current is charge flow rate. An ideal fixed resistor obeys V = IR.
example: A 10 Ω resistor draws 0.5 A at 5 V in an ideal circuit.
misconception: Current is not used up by components in a single series loop.

subject: physics
title: Series and parallel circuits
overview: Series components share current; parallel branches share voltage between common nodes.
example: Two identical resistors in parallel have half the resistance of either alone.
misconception: Adding parallel paths need not increase total resistance.

subject: physics
title: Oscillations and the pendulum
overview: For small swings, pendulum period T ≈ 2π√(L/g). Length affects period more strongly than bob mass in the ideal model.
example: Quadrupling length doubles an ideal pendulum's period.
misconception: The small-angle formula is not accurate for arbitrarily large angles.

subject: physics
title: Wave properties
overview: Wavelength, frequency and wave speed are related by v = fλ in a specified medium.
example: A 2 Hz wave with wavelength 3 m travels at 6 m/s.
misconception: Wave speed does not always stay fixed across different media.

subject: physics
title: Lenses and image formation
overview: Ideal thin lenses follow 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with a specified sign convention. Image character depends on object distance.
example: An object beyond a convex lens focal point can form a real inverted image.
misconception: Magnification is not always positive.

subject: physics
title: Experimental graphs and uncertainty
overview: A graph should label both axes and units. Gradients have physical interpretations only when model assumptions apply.
example: Slope of current versus voltage gives conductance for an ideal ohmic resistor.
misconception: A straight line alone does not prove causation.

subject: biology
title: Cell theory and living cells
overview: Cells are the basic structural and functional units of organisms. Different cell types have specialised structures.
example: Plant cells commonly have a cellulose wall and a large vacuole.
misconception: Not every cell contains a nucleus.

subject: biology
title: Cell organelles
overview: The nucleus stores most eukaryotic genetic material; mitochondria participate in aerobic energy metabolism.
example: Chloroplasts enable photosynthesis in many plant cells.
misconception: All cells do not contain chloroplasts.

subject: biology
title: Microscope magnification
overview: Total magnification is eyepiece magnification multiplied by objective magnification.
example: A ×10 eyepiece with ×40 objective gives ×400.
misconception: Magnification does not guarantee high resolution.

subject: biology
title: Diffusion and osmosis
overview: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient. Osmosis is net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane driven by water potential.
example: A plant cell in a sufficiently hypotonic solution becomes turgid.
misconception: Osmosis is not movement of dissolved sugar across the membrane.

subject: biology
title: Enzymes and metabolic reactions
overview: Enzymes catalyse biochemical reactions. Conditions such as temperature and pH influence their activity.
example: Amylase breaks down starch during digestion.
misconception: Enzymes are not consumed each time they catalyse a reaction.

subject: biology
title: Photosynthesis
overview: Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into organic compounds and releases oxygen in oxygenic organisms.
example: Leaves absorb light and chloroplasts support sugar synthesis.
misconception: Plants also perform cellular respiration.

subject: biology
title: Transpiration and plant transport
overview: Transpiration is water loss as vapour from plant surfaces, often via stomata. A potometer directly tracks water uptake instead.
example: Bubble displacement in a capillary estimates uptake volume.
misconception: Water uptake is not exactly equal to transpiration at every moment.

subject: biology
title: Respiration
overview: Cellular respiration releases usable energy from molecules. Aerobic respiration generally requires oxygen.
example: Mitochondria help generate ATP during aerobic respiration.
misconception: Respiration is not identical to breathing.

subject: biology
title: Inheritance and variation
overview: Genes are inherited DNA sequences; combinations of alleles and environment influence traits.
example: Crosses illustrate predicted genotype ratios under specific assumptions.
misconception: Not every trait follows a single-gene dominant pattern.

subject: biology
title: Classification and ecosystems
overview: Organisms can be classified by shared features and evolutionary relationships. Ecosystems involve organisms and physical conditions.
example: Food webs connect producers, consumers and decomposers.
misconception: An organism can have several food sources and roles.

subject: agriculture
title: Agricultural systems
overview: Agricultural science studies crops, livestock, soil, water and sustainable management of farm resources.
example: A mixed farm raises animals alongside crops.
misconception: Agriculture includes science and management, not only planting.

subject: agriculture
title: Soil composition and texture
overview: Mineral soils contain sand, silt and clay particles along with organic matter, water and air.
example: A soil texture triangle uses sand, silt and clay percentages.
misconception: Soil texture is not the same as soil fertility.

subject: agriculture
title: Soil pH and fertility
overview: Soil pH influences nutrient availability and microbial processes. Fertility also depends on nutrient supply, structure and other conditions.
example: Acidic soils can change how available phosphorus is to plants.
misconception: A single pH reading cannot diagnose every fertility problem.

subject: agriculture
title: Plant nutrients N, P and K
overview: Nitrogen supports proteins and leaves; phosphorus supports energy transfer and development; potassium supports enzyme and water regulation.
example: Older-leaf yellowing can have several possible causes, including nitrogen shortage.
misconception: Leaf appearance alone does not establish a nutrient deficiency.

subject: agriculture
title: Seed germination
overview: A viable seed typically requires suitable moisture, oxygen and temperature to germinate. Species can have additional requirements.
example: Too little water limits imbibition; waterlogging can restrict oxygen.
misconception: More water is not always better for germination.

subject: agriculture
title: Photosynthesis and crop growth
overview: Crop growth depends on photosynthesis, water, mineral nutrition, temperature and disease pressures.
example: Adequate light supports biomass production when other conditions are suitable.
misconception: More fertiliser cannot compensate for every limiting factor.

subject: agriculture
title: Crop pests and diseases
overview: Biotic threats include insects, pathogens and weeds. Identification is needed before choosing a response.
example: Leaf damage can come from pests, disease or environmental stress.
misconception: Visual similarity does not prove the same underlying problem.

subject: agriculture
title: Farm irrigation and water management
overview: Irrigation supplies water when rainfall is insufficient; drainage removes excess water. Scheduling depends on soil and crop.
example: Drip irrigation can direct water near root zones.
misconception: More frequent irrigation is not universally best.

subject: agriculture
title: Livestock nutrition and welfare
overview: Animals require species-appropriate diets, clean water, shelter and health care.
example: Feed requirements differ for ruminants and poultry.
misconception: One ration does not fit every growth stage.

subject: agriculture
title: Farm tools and safe operations
overview: Tools are chosen for specific operations and maintained to reduce accidents and waste.
example: A hoe breaks surface soil; a spade lifts or turns material.
misconception: Protective equipment does not eliminate every machinery hazard.
